profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting in an ML research lab about a PyTorch reimplementation of a quantum-inspired tensor network classifier based on the paper's copy-node initialization and bond-dimension regularization ideas. Over the last week, the team has seen inconsistent behavior: some runs avoid NaNs but still fail to match the reported parameter efficiency or generalization gains, and the latest experiment note says the model is 'stable now' even though downstream results remain erratic. The agenda is to diagnose why the current implementation is not reproducing the expected training behavior, compare what each person means by the recent 'fix,' and decide the next debugging step for the internal benchmark. The expected outcome is agreement on a concrete follow-up experiment and implementation check, even though some second-order assumptions remain misaligned.

members.name: Dr. Nora Iqbal
members.expertise: tensor networks, optimization in quantum-inspired ML, experimental design
members.background: A postdoctoral researcher who led the lab's reading-group reproduction of recent tensor network training papers and designed the current set of benchmark experiments on image classification.
members.private_state: Wants to preserve fidelity to the paper's intended mechanism so the lab can publish a reliable extension, and is worried that engineering shortcuts are masking whether the method itself actually works.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says a run is 'stable,' they mainly mean gradients stay in a healthy range and the loss curve is trainable in the early phase, even before checking seed-robust final accuracy.

Using the 'paper setup' implicitly includes the copy-node initialization together with the same normalization conventions around the tensor cores that were in her notebook, not just the abstract copy-node graph pattern.
The 'baseline' for troubleshooting is the closest paper-faithful no-regularizer ablation from the current project, not the older main-branch implementation from before the rework.

A 'bond-dimension sweep' naturally means trying several regularization strengths while allowing the regularizer to shrink effective ranks during training, because that is the mechanism she wants to validate.

members.name: Evan Chen
members.expertise: PyTorch training pipelines, numerical debugging, experiment infrastructure
members.background: A senior engineer who integrated the tensor network model into the lab's shared training stack, added mixed-precision support, and manages the reproducibility and logging tooling for benchmark runs.
members.private_state: Wants a practical fix that makes the codepath reliable inside the shared pipeline and is concerned about minimizing invasive changes that would break existing experiment tooling or slow large sweeps.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says a run is 'stable,' they mainly mean the training job completes without NaNs, overflows, or catastrophic loss spikes in the full pipeline.

Using the 'same initialization' means loading the same random seed path and copy-node tensor templates; normalization and embedding rescaling are separate preprocessing details unless explicitly called out.
The 'baseline' for comparison is the last trustworthy production-style run in the experiment tracker, which is the pre-rework branch everyone has been using as an operational reference.

A 'bond-dimension sweep' means running a grid over the regularization coefficient while keeping the architecture and pruning behavior fixed, because changing rank adaptation logic at the same time confounds infrastructure comparisons.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a stable run
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to the latest patch as making training 'stable.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the optimization dynamics are healthy in the scientifically relevant sense: non-degenerate gradient norms, smooth early loss descent, and behavior that suggests the initialization/regularizer combination is truly fixing optimization.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the system-level failure mode is gone: the job runs end-to-end without NaNs, AMP overflows, or exploding loss that crashes the trainer.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML troubleshooting, 'stable' is a routine positive shorthand and both see it as obviously desirable; because the latest run did improve on both fronts somewhat, neither feels an immediate need to unpack the exact threshold.

misalignment_points.topic: Which baseline run they are comparing against
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about matching or beating 'the baseline.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is mentally comparing against the paper-faithful no-regularizer ablation run from two weeks ago on the Fashion-MNIST tensorized benchmark with the new core layout.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is mentally comparing against the older main-branch benchmark entry in the tracker from before the reimplementation, which used the lab's previous initialization wrapper and slightly different preprocessing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There is only one commonly discussed 'baseline' in recent Slack threads, so the phrase sounds shared; both runs live in the same tracker under similar tags, making the reference gap easy to miss.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in using the same initialization
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to verify that they used 'the same initialization as in the paper setup.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes the copy-node tensor construction plus the layerwise norm scaling around input and intermediate cores that she treated as part of the initialization recipe when porting her notebook.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes only the copy-node template and random seed path for tensor values; he treats subsequent feature scaling and core renormalization as separate preprocessing or training details.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both parties see the extra normalization as mundane setup rather than a first-class design choice, so the phrase 'same initialization' feels precise enough even though its boundary is different.

misalignment_points.topic: How to do the bond-dimension sweep
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the next step is to 'sweep the bond-dimension regularizer.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 intends to run several values of the regularization strength with the adaptive rank-shrinking update enabled each epoch, because the sweep is supposed to test whether dynamic compression cures the optimization issue.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 intends to run several values of the regularization coefficient while keeping rank adaptation disabled and bond dimensions fixed, because for him a clean sweep changes one logged knob at a time.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: A parameter sweep is a standard phrase that usually does not prompt a discussion of surrounding mechanics; each assumes their preferred execution method is the obvious default for a controlled experiment.
